suggestions.reason: The assertion only checks presence, not the quality of explanations. A model could list all 13 words with a single-word rationale ('bad') and pass. The without_skill model actually wrote substantive critique per flagged word — that quality signal goes unmeasured. Consider adding: 'each flagged item includes a specific reason why it fails (not just that it's a buzzword)'.

No assertion checks whether the explanatory paragraph that follows the rewrite introduces any of the banned words. The executor kept it clean here, but a model could leak 'seamless' or 'robust' into the post-rewrite commentary without failing Expectation 2. Tightening Expectation 2 to cover the full response (not just the blockquoted rewrite) would prevent this.

The assertion set does not check whether the flagged words were actually present in the original input copy. A model fabricating extra slop words not in the original could still pass all assertions. A 'flagged words are a subset of the input copy' check would add meaningful signal.

eval_feedback.overall: All four assertions pass with strong evidence. The rewrite is genuinely good — specific numbers, sentence rhythm variation, and zero slop recycling. The eval's weak point is that Expectation 1 is presence-only: it passes as long as the right words are named, regardless of whether the explanations are substantive or trivial. The other three assertions are well-calibrated.
